tools.name: scene_info
tools.description: Inspect the Blender scene. ALWAYS call this first in a new request and again after big changes. Returns units and scale, frame range, the active/selected objects, the collection tree, and for each object: type, parent, collection, location, rotation (degrees), scale, dimensions (metres, world-space bounding box size), world-space bounding box min/max, vertex/face/triangle counts, material names, modifiers, and shape-key/armature info. Also whole-scene totals and the project directory. Use `names` to inspect only some objects at full detail; use `detail: "summary"` for big scenes.

tools.name: create_primitive
tools.description: Create a mesh primitive (or an empty) with a meaningful `name`. Types: cube, uv_sphere, ico_sphere, cylinder, cone, torus, plane, circle, grid, monkey, empty. Sizes are in metres: `size` is the edge length for cube/plane/grid; `radius` and `depth` (height) for sphere/cylinder/cone/circle; `radius2` is the top radius of a cone/cylinder (0 = point); torus uses `radius` (major) and `minor_radius`. Cylinders and cones are centred on their middle, so a 2 m tall cylinder at z=1 stands on the ground. Pick LOW segment counts for game assets (cylinder 8-12, uv_sphere 12 x 8, ico_sphere subdivisions 1-2). `location` is the object centre. Created objects get smooth shading only if `smooth` is true (default false = flat, best for low-poly).

tools.name: transform_object
tools.description: Move, rotate, scale or resize an existing object, optionally re-parent it. Values are ABSOLUTE unless `relative` is true (then location/rotation are added and scale is multiplied). `rotation_deg` is XYZ Euler in degrees. `dimensions` sets the final world-space size in metres (it rescales the object; use it to hit exact sizes, e.g. a 1.8 m tall character). `apply` bakes transforms into the mesh (list any of location, rotation, scale) - ALWAYS apply scale before export so exported scale is 1. `parent` attaches to another object keeping its world position. Y-up is handled by the glTF exporter; model with Z up in Blender.

tools.name: add_modifier
tools.description: Add, apply or remove a modifier. `action` add (default) | apply | remove. `type` one of BEVEL, SUBSURF, MIRROR, ARRAY, BOOLEAN, SOLIDIFY, DISPLACE, DECIMATE, WEIGHTED_NORMAL, EDGE_SPLIT, TRIANGULATE, SMOOTH, REMESH, WIREFRAME, SCREW, SIMPLE_DEFORM, SHRINKWRAP, CURVE, LATTICE, WAVE, SKIN, MASK. `params` sets modifier properties by their Blender RNA names (snake_case), e.g. BEVEL {width:0.02, segments:2, limit_method:"ANGLE"}; SUBSURF {levels:1, render_levels:2}; MIRROR {use_axis:[true,false,false], use_clip:true, use_mirror_merge:true, mirror_object:"Empty"}; ARRAY {count:5, relative_offset_displace:[1.1,0,0]} or {use_relative_offset:false, use_constant_offset:true, constant_offset_displace:[0,0,0.5]}; BOOLEAN {operation:"DIFFERENCE", object:"Cutter", solver:"EXACT"} (hide the cutter afterwards with transform/run_python display_type or delete it after applying); SOLIDIFY {thickness:0.05, offset:-1}; DECIMATE {ratio:0.5} or {decimate_type:"DISSOLVE", angle_limit:0.1}; DISPLACE {strength:0.3, texture_type:"CLOUDS"} (creates a texture automatically); WEIGHTED_NORMAL {keep_sharp:true}; TRIANGULATE {quad_method:"BEAUTY"}. Unknown property names return the list of valid ones. Objects can be referenced by name. Modifiers are non-destructive: set `apply: true` (or action apply) before export unless the exporter applies them (export_file has `apply_modifiers`). Keep modifier stacks short and name them via `modifier_name`.

tools.name: edit_mesh
tools.description: Edit mesh topology with bmesh using selection DESCRIPTORS (no UI selection needed). `operations` run in order on one object. Each operation: {"op": ..., "select": <selection descriptor>, ...params}. Ops: extrude_faces {offset} (along face normals, metres; negative = inwards); inset_faces {thickness, depth}; bevel {offset, segments, mode:"edge|vert"} (selects edges); loop_cut {axis:"x|y|z", cuts:n, position:optional local coordinate} (slices the whole mesh with evenly spaced planes: a loop cut for boxy shapes); subdivide {cuts, smooth:0..1}; merge_by_distance {distance}; delete {mode:"vert|edge|face"}; translate {offset:[x,y,z]} / scale {factor:[x,y,z] or number, center:"selection|origin"} / rotate {angle_deg, axis:"x|y|z"} on selected vertices; extrude_edges {offset:[x,y,z]}; bridge/fill: fill_hole; dissolve {mode:"limited", angle_deg}; flip_normals; recalc_normals; triangulate; smooth_shading {smooth:true|false}; set_material_index {index}; mark_sharp {angle_deg} (marks edges sharper than the angle). Typical low-poly recipes: tapered trunk = cylinder + scale top faces ({"op":"scale","select":{"mode":"vert","facing"..} }) - or simply use cone/cylinder radius2; windows = inset_faces on a wall face then extrude_faces with a negative offset; roof = cube, translate top verts. The result reports vertex/face/triangle counts before and after and selection sizes, so check that `selected` is not zero (an empty selection is an error unless `allow_empty`).

select.description: Selection descriptor, all given conditions must hold (AND). Omit or {"all":true} for everything. "indices": explicit element indices. "axis_range": {"axis":"x|y|z","min":n,"max":n,"space":"local|world"} on element centres (faces/edges) or vertices. "normal": {"direction":[x,y,z],"min_dot":0.7} for faces (e.g. top faces: direction [0,0,1], min_dot 0.9). "facing": "top|bottom|front|back|left|right" shortcut (front = -Y, back = +Y, right = +X, left = -X, top = +Z). "area": {"min":n,"max":n} face area in local units. "material_index": int. "box": {"min":[x,y,z],"max":[x,y,z]} local-space box containing centres. "invert": true inverts the final result.

mode.description: Element type (default depends on the operation).

tools.name: create_mesh_from_data
tools.description: Create a mesh object from raw geometry: `vertices` [[x,y,z],...] (metres, Z up), `faces` [[i,j,k,...],...] (vertex indices, counter-clockwise when seen from outside so normals point outward; triangles, quads and n-gons OK), optional `uvs` (one [u,v] per face corner in face order). Use for shapes the primitives cannot make (leaves, blades, custom hulls, lathe profiles, terrain patches, you compute the numbers). Up to 200k vertices. Normals are recalculated outward by default.

tools.name: set_material
tools.description: Create or update a PBR material (Principled BSDF) and assign it to one or more objects. `base_color` linear RGB or hex; `metallic` 0..1 (0 for wood/plastic/skin/foliage, 1 for bare metal); `roughness` 0..1; `alpha` (<1 enables blending); `emission` {color, strength}; `ior`; `transmission` for glass; `coat`; `normal_strength`. `texture` adds a PROCEDURAL texture driving a channel: {type: noise|voronoi|wave|checker|brick|gradient|magic, target: base_color|roughness|bump|emission|metallic, scale, detail, distortion, color1, color2, strength}. For base_color/emission the texture blends color1->color2; for roughness/metallic it blends 0.3..0.9 style numbers via color1/color2 greyscale; for bump it perturbs normals. Procedural nodes DO NOT survive glTF export: for game assets prefer plain `base_color`/`roughness` (flat or vertex-coloured low-poly look) and say so. `slot` picks a material slot index (default: replace slot 0 or append). Re-using a `material` name edits that material, so identical looks share one material (game-ready: few materials). `double_sided` disables backface culling (leaves, planes).

base_color.description: Linear RGB(A) 0..1 as [r,g,b] / [r,g,b,a], or a hex string like "#3a7d2c" (sRGB hex, converted).

color.description: Linear RGB(A) 0..1 as [r,g,b] / [r,g,b,a], or a hex string like "#3a7d2c" (sRGB hex, converted).

color1.description: Linear RGB(A) 0..1 as [r,g,b] / [r,g,b,a], or a hex string like "#3a7d2c" (sRGB hex, converted).

color2.description: Linear RGB(A) 0..1 as [r,g,b] / [r,g,b,a], or a hex string like "#3a7d2c" (sRGB hex, converted).

tools.name: assign_collection
tools.description: Move objects into a collection (created if missing) - the way to organise a scene and to choose what gets exported (e.g. a collection "Tree_LOD0"). `exclusive` (default true) unlinks them from their other collections. `parent_collection` nests a new collection. Use short PascalCase/snake_case names.

tools.name: set_origin
tools.description: Move an object's pivot (origin) without moving the geometry in the world. `mode`: bottom_center (origin at the middle of the bottom of the bounding box: the convention for props, characters and trees that stand on the ground), center_bounds, center_mass, world_origin, location (use `location`, world space). Game convention: origin at the base, object placed at the world origin or its intended position, scale applied (1,1,1), +Y forward in Godot = -Y in Blender (the glTF exporter converts axes, do not rotate for that).

tools.name: uv_unwrap
tools.description: Generate UV coordinates for mesh objects. `method`: smart_project (default, good for hard-surface/low-poly; `angle_limit_deg` ~66), angle_based (conformal, organic, needs seams), cube_project, cylinder_project, sphere_project. `island_margin` 0.001..0.05 prevents bleeding in small textures. Run before export if the asset uses textures; flat-colour low-poly assets need no UVs. Reports islands/overlap-free status as vertex counts only.

tools.name: import_file
tools.description: Import a glb/gltf/obj/fbx/stl/blend(append objects) file located INSIDE the project directory (relative path or absolute path under it). Imported objects are returned by name. `collection` puts them in a collection; `scale` multiplies size.

tools.name: export_file
tools.description: Export to glb/gltf/obj/fbx/stl or save a .blend, ONLY inside the project directory (relative paths; "../" and absolute paths outside are refused). `format` glb (default; best for Godot: single binary file), gltf, obj, fbx, stl, blend. `objects` limits what is exported (default: everything visible, or the `collection`). glTF export applies Y-up conversion for you, keeps materials (Principled BSDF factors, image textures; procedural nodes are not exported), uses `apply_modifiers` (default true), optional `animations`. Run `check_game_ready` first, apply scale, and name the file after the asset (e.g. "models/tree_pine.glb").

tools.name: set_camera
tools.description: Create or update a camera and (by default) make it the scene camera. Give `location` and either `look_at` (a world point; recommended) or `rotation_deg`. `lens` focal length in mm (35-50 natural; 85 for portraits), `ortho` true with `ortho_scale` for isometric/game-style views (isometric: rotation [60,0,45], ortho). For a good product-style shot, place the camera about 2.5x the object size away, 20-35 degrees above, looking at the object centre.

tools.name: set_light
tools.description: Create or update a light. `type`: SUN (direction via `rotation_deg` or `look_at`; energy ~2-5 W/m2), POINT, SPOT (`spot_size_deg`), AREA (`size`; soft key lights). `energy` is in watts (point/area/spot hundreds-1000 W for room-scale scenes; a sun is strength 1-6). Classic 3-point setup: key (area, 45 degrees to the side/above), fill (weaker, opposite), rim (behind). `color` linear RGB or hex.

color.description: Linear RGB(A) 0..1 as [r,g,b] / [r,g,b,a], or a hex string like "#3a7d2c" (sRGB hex, converted).

tools.name: set_world
tools.description: Set the world (background/ambient light): `color` flat colour, or `sky_gradient` {horizon, zenith} colours (a quick studio/sky look), with `strength` (0.3-1.5 usual). `transparent` makes renders have a transparent background (useful for sprites/icons). `unit_system`/`unit_scale` set scene units (default metric, scale 1.0 = 1 unit is 1 m: keep 1.0 for game export).

color.description: Linear RGB(A) 0..1 as [r,g,b] / [r,g,b,a], or a hex string like "#3a7d2c" (sRGB hex, converted).

horizon.description: Linear RGB(A) 0..1 as [r,g,b] / [r,g,b,a], or a hex string like "#3a7d2c" (sRGB hex, converted).

zenith.description: Linear RGB(A) 0..1 as [r,g,b] / [r,g,b,a], or a hex string like "#3a7d2c" (sRGB hex, converted).

tools.name: viewport_screenshot
tools.description: LOOK at the scene. Returns a PNG image you can see. Use it after every meaningful change and critique silhouette, proportions, floating/intersecting parts, flipped normals (dark faces) and colour. `view`: perspective (default 3/4 view), front (looks along +Y), back, right, left, top, bottom, camera (the scene camera). `focus`: all (default), selected, or an object name list in `objects`. `shading`: solid (default, with matcap-style lighting), wireframe (shows topology: use to check poly density), material (colours/materials). Max 1024 px, default 640. This renders offscreen so it works without a visible 3D view.

tools.name: render_preview
tools.description: Render the scene camera to a PNG you can see (lit, with materials, shadows and the world). Capped at 1280 px and low samples so it is fast. `engine`: auto (Cycles on the CPU: reliable everywhere, a few seconds), eevee (GPU), cycles, workbench (GPU). If there is no camera one is created and framed on the scene. `save_to` optionally writes the PNG inside the project directory. Use it for final beauty checks; use viewport_screenshot for fast iteration.

tools.name: delete_object
tools.description: Delete objects by name (optionally with children). Their orphaned mesh data and unused materials are purged. Deleting is undoable with the `undo` tool.

tools.name: undo
tools.description: Undo. `steps` (default 1) undo steps, or `checkpoint: "request_start"` to return to the state saved at the start of the user's current request (the safe way to abandon a failed approach).

tools.name: duplicate_object
tools.description: Duplicate an object (`linked: true` shares mesh data: cheaper and keeps edits in sync, good for repeated props). Returns the new name. Optionally offset it.

tools.name: set_shading
tools.description: Set flat or smooth shading on mesh objects. `mode`: flat (faceted low-poly), smooth, auto (smooth but keeps edges sharper than `angle_deg` crisp; best for most hard-surface and stylised assets).

tools.name: check_game_ready
tools.description: Audit objects against the game-ready checklist and return concrete problems: unapplied scale/rotation, negative scale, triangle budget (`budget_tris`), n-gons, loose geometry, non-manifold edges, missing/duplicate UVs when textured, too many materials, default names ("Cube.003"), origin far from the base, unapplied modifiers, tiny/huge size. Fix what it lists, then call it again until `ok` is true, then export_file.

tools.name: create_armature
tools.description: Create an armature from a bone list for simple rigs. `bones`: [{name, head:[x,y,z], tail:[x,y,z], parent:name?, connect?:bool}] in world metres. Optionally bind meshes (`bind` names) with automatic weights. Typical humanoid: Hips, Spine, Chest, Neck, Head, Upper/Lower arm and leg L/R with `.L`/`.R` suffixes (Godot-friendly names). Keep bone counts low.

tools.name: pose_keyframes
tools.description: Create an animation clip (an Action) by keyframing bone rotations/locations: {armature, action: "walk", frame_start, frame_end, loop, keyframes:[{frame, bones:{BoneName:{rotation_deg:[x,y,z], location:[x,y,z]}}}]}. Rotations are local Euler XYZ degrees relative to the rest pose. For a 24 fps walk cycle: 25 frames, contact/passing/contact poses, last frame = first frame when `loop`. Name clips idle, walk, run, attack so Godot imports them as named animations. Use `preset` (idle|walk|attack) to auto-generate a simple clip for armatures that follow the humanoid naming of create_armature; you can still pass keyframes to refine.

tools.name: run_python
tools.description: LAST RESORT: run generated Blender Python (bpy/bmesh/mathutils/math/random/colorsys/itertools/collections only) when no structured tool can do the job, e.g. procedural geometry, many-object scatter, curves, lattice-like loops. The code is statically checked (no os/sys/subprocess/socket/ctypes, no open/eval/exec/__import__, no dunder or escape attributes, no bpy.ops.wm/script/import_/export_, no bpy.app/utils/path), shown to the user for approval when review mode is on, time-limited (20 s) and its print() output is returned. Do NOT try to read/write files or open the network. Prefer bmesh over bpy.ops for geometry (ops need UI context). Name every object you create, put results in variables and print() the names/counts so you can verify. `bpy`, `bmesh`, `mathutils`, `math`, `random`, `C` (context) and `D` (data) are pre-imported.
